## Desired behavior
https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sim/pull/3957 introduced component registration for Python. It requires calling a macro for each component rather than tieing into `GZ_SIM_REGISTER_COMPONENT`. 

## Alternatives considered
<!-- Describe alternate solutions or features you've considered.-->

## Implementation suggestion
https://github.com/gazebosim/gz-sim/pull/3957#discussion_r4163079001 suggests a way to automate this. However, we have to consider how that would work for components registered by end-users in cases where they don't want the component to be registered in Python (e.g. the contained data doesn't have pybind11 bindings).

## Additional context
<!-- Provide any other additional context (e.g., screenshots) about your feature
request.-->
new_candidates.title: Automate registration of components in Python

new_candidates.body:
### Intro

Hi!

I am a researcher working on sim-to-real manipulation policy training
[optionally add your affiliation]. I use MuJoCo (CPU) as my deployment /
reference engine and `mujoco_warp` (GPU) for large-scale RL training of the
same tasks, and I am trying to understand how much behavioral divergence
between the two engines is expected.

### My setup

- mujoco `3.15.0` (Python API) and `mujoco_warp` `3.15.0`, Warp `1.17.0`
- GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (sm_120), CUDA 12.9, driver 13.0
- OS: x86_64 Linux (kernel 5.15), Python 3.10

### What's happening? What did you expect?


In a contact-rich closed-loop manipulation workload (7-DOF arm, ~20
simultaneous self-collision/table contacts, elliptic friction cones,
`impratio=10`, equality-coupled gripper joints), the **same trained policy**
driven by the two engines produces very different success rates on a fixed
set of 500 seeds:

- `mujoco_warp` (GPU, f32): 99.6%
- `mujoco` (CPU, f64): 87.4%

The CPU-side failures are almost exclusively end-of-episode stalls near the
place pose (cube still held, ~9 cm short of the target, episode times out;
~45% of failures show joint-limit saturation).

To localize this, I ran white-box comparisons of the two engines at
identical states, and found the opposite of what I expected — the engines
appear to **agree exactly at the single-step level**:

1. Same model, same full state (all qpos/qvel/ctrl/mocap rows copied,
   `qacc_warmstart` zeroed on both sides) at a loaded static arm pose with
   20 active contacts: `qfrc_actuator` and `qfrc_constraint` match to
   Δmax = 0.0000 N·m.
2. Along an open-loop rollout of the minimal model below (identical initial
   state and ctrl, no re-synchronization): per-step
   `|Δqfrc_constraint| ≤ 7e-5 N·m` at every probed checkpoint, and
   `|Δqpos|max` grows only from 2.4e-8 to 4.7e-5 over 3000 steps (6 s).

So the single-step solvers agree (to f32 precision), the minimal open-loop
drift stays at machine-epsilon scale, yet the closed-loop, contact-rich
behavioral gap in our workload is large and systematic.

What I expected / am asking: is a divergence of this magnitude between
`mujoco` (f64) and `mujoco_warp` (f32) considered expected behavior once a
feedback policy is in the loop (f32 rounding accumulating through contact
discontinuities and the policy reacting to the diverged states), or is this
worth investigating as an unintended engine difference? Are there
recommended practices (beyond training with force/parameter randomization,
which we already do) for keeping policies trained on `mujoco_warp`
transferable to CPU `mujoco`?


**Related prior issues (searched before filing)**

- #318 "Mismatch between mjc and mjwarp rollouts" (closed, May 2025,
  mujoco 3.3.3.dev): single-step `qpos` mismatch ~1e-2 in a
  cylinder-push contact example, plus NaN at zero friction. On 3.15.0 our
  single-step force comparisons at identical states agree to 0.0000 /
  f32-epsilon (see above), so that class of single-step mismatch appears
  to have improved since.
- #562 "Determinism" (open, on the MJWarp roadmap, PR #1687): run-to-run
  determinism for warp; the mjlab FAQ links it ("MuJoCo Warp does not yet
  guarantee determinism"). Our question is adjacent but different:
  cross-engine (f64 CPU vs f32 GPU) closed-loop divergence, not
  run-to-run.
- #505 "Instabilities with MJWarp in Grasping Scenario" (closed): CPU
  MuJoCo stable vs warp unstable (integrator / eulerdamp / mesh
  dependent) in a fingertip-grasp task — the closest prior report to our
  workload, but framed as instability rather than a quantified
  closed-loop performance gap.
- #1455 (open, Jun 2026): mesh-vs-SDF collision behavior differs between
  the two engines.
- mujoco#892 "Add support for double precision floats" (2020): the
  long-standing f32 limitation request.

I did not find a prior report combining (a) bit-level single-step force
parity at identical states with (b) a quantified closed-loop policy
performance gap between the two engines — which is what this issue adds.

### Steps for reproduction


1. Save the script below as `repro_warp_rollout_divergence.py` (the MJCF is
   embedded in the `MJCF` string; also reproduced separately above).
2. Run `MUJOCO_GL=egl CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python
   repro_warp_rollout_divergence.py`.
3. Observed output (my machine, quoted in full below): at every checkpoint
   the parity probe reports `|Δqfrc_constraint|max` ≤ 7e-5 N·m between the
   two engines at the identical state, while the independently integrated
   open-loop trajectories drift apart only at f32-epsilon scale
   (`|Δqpos|max` 2.4e-8 → 4.7e-5 over 6 s).

The script is self-contained (primitive geometry only, no external assets).
It demonstrates the single-step agreement and the epsilon-scale open-loop
drift; the large closed-loop gap reported above is from a proprietary robot
scene that I cannot attach, but on that full model the same single-step
parity checks also hold bit-exactly at a 20-contact static state.

### Minimal model for reproduction


A 7-link capsule chain with hinge joints and damping, self-collision enabled
between non-parent-child links, a free box on the floor, one `equality/joint`
coupling (mimicking a gripper transmission), `cone="elliptic"`,
`impratio="10"`, `solver="Newton"`, `integrator="implicitfast"`,
`timestep=0.002` — embedded in the script below (`MJCF` string) and listed
in the collapsible section here:

<details><summary>minimal XML</summary>

```XML
<mujoco model="minpress">
  <option timestep="0.002" gravity="0 0 -9.81" integrator="implicitfast"
          solver="Newton" iterations="80" cone="elliptic" impratio="10"/>
  <compiler angle="radian"/>
  <worldbody>
    <geom name="floor" type="plane" size="2 2 0.1"/>
    <body name="l1" pos="0 0 0.50">
      <joint name="j1" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-1.5 1.5" damping="1.0"/>
      <geom name="g1" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.28 0 0" size="0.045"/>
      <body name="l2" pos="0.28 0 0">
        <joint name="j2" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
        <geom name="g2" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.24 0 0" size="0.040"/>
        <body name="l3" pos="0.24 0 0">
          <joint name="j3" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
          <geom name="g3" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.20 0 0" size="0.037"/>
          <body name="l4" pos="0.20 0 0">
            <joint name="j4" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
            <geom name="g4" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.17 0 0" size="0.034"/>
            <body name="l5" pos="0.17 0 0">
              <joint name="j5" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
              <geom name="g5" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.14 0 0" size="0.032"/>
              <body name="l6" pos="0.14 0 0">
                <joint name="j6" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
                <geom name="g6" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.11 0 0" size="0.030"/>
                <body name="l7" pos="0.11 0 0">
                  <joint name="j7" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
                  <geom name="g7" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.09 0 0" size="0.028"/>
                </body>
              </body>
            </body>
          </body>
        </body>
      </body>
    </body>
    <body name="box" pos="0.60 0 0.050">
      <freejoint name="bj"/>
      <geom name="gb" type="box" size="0.06 0.06 0.050"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
  <equality>
    <joint joint1="j6" joint2="j7" polycoef="0 1 0 0 0"/>
  </equality>
  <actuator>
    <motor name="m1" joint="j1" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m2" joint="j2" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m3" joint="j3" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m4" joint="j4" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m5" joint="j5" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m6" joint="j6" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
  </actuator>
</mujoco>
```

</details>

### Code required for reproduction


```python
# repro_warp_rollout_divergence.py
# Open-loop divergence demo + single-step parity probes:
# mujoco (CPU, f64) vs mujoco_warp (GPU, f32), identical model/state/ctrl.
import os
import sys

os.environ.setdefault("MUJOCO_GL", "egl")

import numpy as np
import mujoco
import warp as wp
import mujoco_warp as mjw

MJCF = """
<mujoco model="minpress">
  <option timestep="0.002" gravity="0 0 -9.81" integrator="implicitfast"
          solver="Newton" iterations="80" cone="elliptic" impratio="10"/>
  <compiler angle="radian"/>
  <worldbody>
    <geom name="floor" type="plane" size="2 2 0.1"/>
    <body name="l1" pos="0 0 0.50">
      <joint name="j1" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-1.5 1.5" damping="1.0"/>
      <geom name="g1" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.28 0 0" size="0.045"/>
      <body name="l2" pos="0.28 0 0">
        <joint name="j2" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
        <geom name="g2" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.24 0 0" size="0.040"/>
        <body name="l3" pos="0.24 0 0">
          <joint name="j3" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
          <geom name="g3" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.20 0 0" size="0.037"/>
          <body name="l4" pos="0.20 0 0">
            <joint name="j4" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
            <geom name="g4" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.17 0 0" size="0.034"/>
            <body name="l5" pos="0.17 0 0">
              <joint name="j5" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
              <geom name="g5" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.14 0 0" size="0.032"/>
              <body name="l6" pos="0.14 0 0">
                <joint name="j6" type="hinge" axis="0 0 1" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
                <geom name="g6" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.11 0 0" size="0.030"/>
                <body name="l7" pos="0.11 0 0">
                  <joint name="j7" type="hinge" axis="0 1 0" range="-2.0 2.0" damping="1.0"/>
                  <geom name="g7" type="capsule" fromto="0 0 0 0.09 0 0" size="0.028"/>
                </body>
              </body>
            </body>
          </body>
        </body>
      </body>
    </body>
    <body name="box" pos="0.60 0 0.050">
      <freejoint name="bj"/>
      <geom name="gb" type="box" size="0.06 0.06 0.050"/>
    </body>
  </worldbody>
  <equality>
    <joint joint1="j6" joint2="j7" polycoef="0 1 0 0 0"/>
  </equality>
  <actuator>
    <motor name="m1" joint="j1" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m2" joint="j2" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m3" joint="j3" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m4" joint="j4" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m5" joint="j5" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
    <motor name="m6" joint="j6" ctrlrange="-40 40"/>
  </actuator>
</mujoco>
"""

CTRL = np.array([16.0, 20.0, 14.0, 18.0, 12.0, 10.0])
N_STEPS = 3000
CHECKS = (0, 100, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000)


def main():
    m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(MJCF)
    d = mujoco.MjData(m)
    d.qpos[:] = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0.60, 0, 0.05, 1, 0, 0, 0]
    d.qvel[:] = 0
    d.ctrl[:] = CTRL
    mujoco.mj_forward(m, d)

    wp.init()
    with wp.ScopedDevice(wp.get_device("cuda:0")):
        wm = mjw.put_model(m)
        wd = mjw.put_data(m, d)

    def parity_probe(tag):
        # copy full CPU state into warp, one forward on each, compare forces
        wd.qpos.assign(d.qpos.astype(np.float32))
        wd.qvel.assign(d.qvel.astype(np.float32))
        wd.ctrl.assign(d.ctrl.astype(np.float32))
        wd.qacc_warmstart.zero_()
        d2 = mujoco.MjData(m)
        d2.qpos[:] = d.qpos
        d2.qvel[:] = d.qvel
        d2.ctrl[:] = d.ctrl
        mujoco.mj_forward(m, d2)
        mjw.forward(wm, wd)
        fc = d2.qfrc_constraint.copy()
        fg = np.array(wd.qfrc_constraint.numpy())
        print(f"[div] parity@{tag}: ncon(cpu)={d2.ncon}  "
              f"|dqfrc_constraint|max={np.abs(fg - fc).max():.3e}")

    print(f"[div] versions: mujoco={mujoco.__version__} "
          f"warp={wp.config.version}  steps={N_STEPS} (dt=0.002)")
    for k in range(N_STEPS + 1):
        if k in CHECKS:
            qpos_g = np.array(wd.qpos.numpy()).astype(np.float64)
            dq = np.abs(qpos_g - d.qpos).max()
            dv = np.abs(np.array(wd.qvel.numpy()).astype(np.float64)
                        - d.qvel).max()
            print(f"[div] step {k:5d} ({k*2:5d} ms): "
                  f"|dqpos|max={dq:.3e}  |dqvel|max={dv:.3e}  ncon={d.ncon}")
            if k > 0:
                parity_probe(f"step{k}")
        if k == N_STEPS:
            break
        mujoco.mj_step(m, d)          # f64 CPU integrates
        mjw.step(wm, wd)              # f32 GPU integrates
    print("[div] done")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Observed output (RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, mujoco 3.15.0 / mujoco_warp
3.15.0 / Warp 1.17.0):

```text
[div] step     0 (    0 ms): |dqpos|max=2.384e-08  |dqvel|max=0.000e+00  ncon=4
[div] step   100 (  200 ms): |dqpos|max=7.510e-07  |dqvel|max=3.455e-06  ncon=4
[div] parity@step100: ncon(cpu)=4  |dqfrc_constraint|max=5.614e-06
[div] step   500 ( 1000 ms): |dqpos|max=6.378e-07  |dqvel|max=9.056e-06  ncon=5
[div] parity@step500: ncon(cpu)=5  |dqfrc_constraint|max=4.445e-05
[div] step  1000 ( 2000 ms): |dqpos|max=5.593e-06  |dqvel|max=3.016e-05  ncon=5
[div] parity@step1000: ncon(cpu)=5  |dqfrc_constraint|max=5.537e-05
[div] step  2000 ( 4000 ms): |dqpos|max=2.059e-05  |dqvel|max=4.545e-05  ncon=5
[div] parity@step2000: ncon(cpu)=5  |dqfrc_constraint|max=6.787e-05
[div] step  3000 ( 6000 ms): |dqpos|max=4.681e-05  |dqvel|max=5.703e-05  ncon=5
[div] parity@step3000: ncon(cpu)=5  |dqfrc_constraint|max=6.087e-05
[div] done
```

### Confirmations

- [x] I searched the [latest documentation](https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/latest/overview.html) thoroughly before posting.
- [x] I searched previous [Issues](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco/issues) and [Discussions](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco/discussions), I am certain this has not been raised before.
new_candidates.title: Same policy, same seeds: 99.6% on mujoco_warp vs 87.4% on mujoco — per-step forces bit-identical, closed-loop behavior diverges

new_candidates.body:
**Describe the bug**
When a hardware component is `active` and its `write()` (or `read()`) method returns `hardware_interface::return_type::ERROR`, the framework correctly invokes the component's `on_error()` callback. If `on_error()` returns `CallbackReturn::SUCCESS`, the component enters the `unconfigured` state.

This is expected behavior and works correctly (the output of `ros2 control list_hardware_components` indicates that the hardware component is `unconfigured`).

However, the `/controller_manager/activity` topic doesn't update to reflect the transition to `unconfigured`. It continues to falsely report `active` (which conflicts with the output of the above `ros2 control` command).

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a hardware component with where the `write()` function errors, and `on_error()` successfully recovers:
```cpp
hardware_interface::return_type
MyHardware::write(const rclcpp::Time &, const rclcpp::Duration &) {
  RCLCPP_WARN(get_logger(), "You've made me upset... going to return an error");
  return hardware_interface::return_type::ERROR;
}

rclcpp_lifecycle::node_interfaces::LifecycleNodeInterface::CallbackReturn
MyHardware::on_error(const rclcpp_lifecycle::State & previous_state) {
  RCLCPP_ERROR(get_logger(), "on_error called. Recovering");
  return rclcpp_lifecycle::node_interfaces::LifecycleNodeInterface::CallbackReturn::SUCCESS;
}
```
2. Run `ros2 topic echo /controller_manager/activity --qos-durability=transient_local`
3. In another window, run the controller manager node with the hardware component.
4. Once activated, the component immediately errors when it enters the write loop. Observe the "going to return an error" and "on_error called" messages in the logs.
5. Run `ros2 control list_hardware_components` and observe that the hardware component is `unconfigured`.
6. Return to the output of the `/controller_manager/activity` topic and note that the hardware component's state is still `active`.


**Expected behavior**
After the `CallbackReturn::SUCCESS` from the `on_error` callback, the controller manager should publish a message to `controller_manager/activity` with the updated state of the hardware component.

**Environment**
 - OS: Ubuntu 24.04.5
 - Version: Jazzy
 - ros2_control: 4.48.1-1noble.20261006.040510

**Additional context**
Apologies if these steps to reproduce aren't clear enough. I unfortunately can't provide the exact code, as it is a work-related closed-source project. However, if needed, I could make a more thorough example.


**Suspected Culprit**
The Controller Manager sets the Resource Manager's `on_component_state_switch_callback` to [`publish_activity`](https://github.com/ros-controls/ros2_control/blob/a58dbe323ed58531c63d35662d860b8abfe01e4f/controller_manager/src/controller_manager.cpp#L663), which is then called at the end of [`set_component_state()`](https://github.com/ros-controls/ros2_control/blob/cc6bbd666e9bc6435cc5544b29f1c52a068f6fe2/hardware_interface/src/resource_manager.cpp#L661-L664) to make sure that the activity topic gets updated whenever a component changes states. 

I think the cause of the bug is from the way that `ResourceManager::read()` and `ResourceManager::write()` handle the `ERROR` return value. 

They call `component.error()` at [here](https://github.com/ros-controls/ros2_control/blob/cc6bbd666e9bc6435cc5544b29f1c52a068f6fe2/hardware_interface/src/resource_manager.cpp#L2509) and [here](https://github.com/ros-controls/ros2_control/blob/cc6bbd666e9bc6435cc5544b29f1c52a068f6fe2/hardware_interface/src/resource_manager.cpp#L2608) respectively, and don't use the `set_component_state()` function that other parts of the resource manager use (for example, the handler for `DEACTIVATE` return value from `write()` uses [`set_component_state()`](https://github.com/ros-controls/ros2_control/blob/cc6bbd666e9bc6435cc5544b29f1c52a068f6fe2/hardware_interface/src/resource_manager.cpp#L2617) to change states). Since they don't use `set_component_state()`, they never end up calling the `on_component_state_switch_callback_()` that updates the activity topic.

I'm assuming the choice to use `component.error()` instead of `set_component_state()` was a deliberate design choice that I just don't understand. I think the fix for this would just be adding the call to `on_component_state_switch_callback_()` after the `component.error()` calls:

```cpp
if (on_component_state_switch_callback_) 
{
  on_component_state_switch_callback_();
}
```
new_candidates.title: `controller_manager/activity` doesn't update after handling hardware error
